content_html:
A hidden leak may first appear as higher water use, dampness, odor, mold, or meter movement when no water is intentionally running. The most useful approach is to confirm unexplained water use and then isolate areas rather than opening walls blindly.

Rule out visible water use and appliances first

Turn off faucets and avoid using the washer, dishwasher, irrigation, or ice maker during the test. Check toilets because a leaking fill or flush valve can move the meter without leaving a visible puddle.

Watch the water meter during a no-use period

Record the meter reading or flow indicator and wait without using water. Persistent movement suggests hidden use; make sure no automatic equipment cycled before concluding that a leak exists.

Look for moisture, odor, and material changes

Bubbling paint, swollen trim, a warm or damp floor, musty odor, and expanding stains can narrow the location. A moisture meter can compare areas but does not by itself identify which pipe is leaking.

Isolate branches before opening finishes

Closing an identified irrigation, water-heater, or branch valve can show whether meter movement stops. If the leak remains hidden, acoustic or thermal leak detection can reduce demolition; water near electricity requires power isolation from a dry location.
